Also called placental abruption; a disorder in which the placenta separates from the uterine wall before the birth of the fetus. Abruption means breaking off. Can cause fetal death or long-term health complications.

An abnormal absence of menstrual periods for 90 days or more. Normal only before puberty, during pregnancy, while breastfeeding, and after menopause; can be caused by stress, hormonal problems, inadequate nutrition, or excessive exercise.
breakdown_text: a-: without ; men/o: menstruation ; -rrhea: flow or discharge

definition: Abbreviated AMN; a surgical puncture with a needle to obtain a specimen of amniotic fluid. The specimen, usually obtained after the 15th week of pregnancy, is used to evaluate fetal health and to diagnose certain congenital disorders.
breakdown_text: amni/o: amnion and fetal membrane ; -centesis: a surgical puncture to remove fluid

definition: Sometimes referred to as male menopause; marked by the decrease of the male hormone testosterone. The gradual hormonal change usually begins when a man is in his 40s, and can cause low energy, depression, a reduction in muscle mass, and difficulty sleeping or concentrating. Androgen is a male sex hormone.

A scale of 1 to 10 to evaluate a newborn infant's physical status at 1 and 5 minutes after birth. Named for obstetrical anesthesiologist Virginia Apgar. The newborn is evaluated by assigning values (0, 1 or 2) to each of five criteria: heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflexes, and skin color. A total score of 8 to 10 indicates the best possible condition.
The absence of sperm in the semen.
breakdown_text: a-: without ; zoo: life ; sperm: sperm ; -ia: abnormal condition

definition: The presence of precancerous changes in the cells that make up the inner lining of the cervix. Without early detection and treatment, these cells can become malignant.
An inflammation of the cervix that is usually caused by infection, irritation or allergies.

A sexually transmitted disease caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis; the most commonly reported STD in the United States. Highly contagious and requires early treatment with antibiotics. In females it can damage the reproductive organs, and serious complications can cause irreversible damage, including infertility; in males it is one of the causes of urethritis.

Abbreviated CVS; the examination of cells retrieved from the chorionic villi, which are minute, vascular projections on the chorion. Performed between the 11th and 14th weeks of pregnancy to search for genetic abnormalities in the developing fetus.

A specialized form of breast milk that delivers essential nutrients and antibodies in a form that the newborn can digest. Produced by the mammary glands in late pregnancy and during the first few days after giving birth.
The surgical suturing of a tear in the vaginal wall.
The direct visual examination of the tissues of the cervix, vagina and vulva. Performed using a binocular magnifier known as a colposcope.
Or menstrual cramps; pain caused by uterine contractions during a menstrual period. The pain, which occurs in the lower abdomen, can be sharp, intermittent, dull, or aching.
breakdown_text: dys-: bad ; men/o: menstruation ; -rrhea: flow or discharge

definition: A serious condition characterized by seizures and coma that can develop from uncontrolled preeclampsia, during or after pregnancy.
Also known as an extrauterine pregnancy; a dangerous condition in which a fertilized egg is implanted and begins to develop outside of the uterus. Ectopic means out of place.
A condition in which patches of endometrial tissue escape the uterus and become attached to other structures in the pelvic cavity. The cause of this painful condition is not known.
breakdown_text: endo-: within ; metri: uterus ; -osis: abnormal condition

definition: A painful inflammation of the epididymis resulting from a bacterial infection. The most common cause is sexually transmitted diseases such as gonorrhea or chlamydia; urinary tract infections can also cause it.
A surgical incision made into the perineum to enlarge the vaginal orifice to prevent tearing of the tissues as the infant moves out of the birth canal.

A round, firm, rubbery mass that arises from excess growth of glandular and connective tissue in the breast. Benign and usually painless; occurs most often between ages 15 and 35. Often enlarges during pregnancy and shrinks after menopause due to changes in hormone levels.
breakdown_text: fibr/o: fibrous tissue ; aden: gland ; -oma: tumor

definition: The production of breast milk in a woman who is not breastfeeding. Caused by a malfunction of the pituitary gland.

A highly contagious sexually transmitted disease caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae. In women it affects the vagina and reproductive tract; in both men and women it can affect the urethra, causing painful urination and an abnormal discharge, as well as the mouth, throat, rectum or joints.
The presence of blood in the semen. Can be caused by infections of the seminal vesicles, prostatitis, urethritis, or urethral strictures.
breakdown_text: hemat/o: relating to blood ; sperm: sperm ; -ia: abnormal condition

definition: A fluid-filled sac in the scrotum along the spermatic cord leading from the testicles. Most common in newborns, especially premature infants, and usually disappears without treatment. The term is also used to describe the accumulation of fluid in any body cavity.
breakdown_text: hydr/o: relating to water ; -cele: a hernia or swelling

definition: An unusually small amount of menstrual flow during a shortened regular menstrual period.
breakdown_text: hypo-: deficient ; men/o: menstruation ; -rrhea: flow or discharge

definition: The surgical removal of the uterus, often due to problems caused by uterine fibroids, gynecological cancer, endometriosis, or uterine prolapse. Further described by the structures that are removed.

Abbreviated HSG; an x-ray examination of the uterus and fallopian tubes. Requires the instillation of radiopaque contrast material into the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes to make them visible. Instillation means the slow introduction of a liquid into a body part by pouring or injection.
breakdown_text: hyster/o: uterus ; salping/o: fallopian tube ; -graphy: the process of producing a picture or record

definition: Abbreviated HYS; the direct visual examination of the interior of the uterus and fallopian tubes. Used to diagnose and treat abnormal bleeding, performed by using the lighted magnification of a hysteroscope.
The process of forming and secreting milk from the breasts as nourishment for the infant. The breast milk develops a few days after giving birth to replace the colostrum.

A whitish mucus discharge from the uterus and vagina. Women normally may have some vaginal discharge; leukorrhea describes a change and increase in this discharge that may be due to an infection or hormonal imbalance.
Pain in the breast.
Also called a breast lift; elective surgery to affix sagging breasts in a more elevated position.
The beginning of menstruation. Begins after the maturation that occurs during puberty.
Also known as intermenstrual bleeding; excessive uterine bleeding at both the usual time of menstrual periods and at other irregular intervals.
breakdown_text: men/o: menstruation ; metr/o: uterus ; -rrhagia: abnormal bleeding

definition: The newborn infant during the first 4 weeks after birth.
A woman who has never borne a viable child.
Abbreviated OB; a physician who specializes in providing medical care to women during pregnancy, childbirth, and immediately thereafter. This specialty is referred to as obstetrics.
Also called infrequent menstruation; irregular or very light menstruation in a woman with previously normal periods. Oligomenorrhea is the opposite of polymenorrhea.
breakdown_text: olig/o: scanty ; men/o: menstruation ; -rrhea: flow or discharge

definition: Also known as an ovariectomy; the surgical removal of one or both ovaries. If both ovaries are removed in a premenopausal woman, the patient will experience surgical menopause because the hormone estrogen is no longer being produced.
Also spelled orchidectomy; the surgical removal of one or both testicles.

The repair of cryptorchidism, which is an undescended testicle. An endoscopic surgery performed on infants before the age of 1 year to move the testicle into its normal position in the scrotum; also used to resolve testicular torsion.

Abbreviated PID; any inflammation of the female reproductive organs that is not associated with surgery or pregnancy. Occurs most frequently as a complication of a sexually transmitted disease and can lead to infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and other serious disorders.

The transition phase between regular menstrual periods and no periods at all. Can last as long as a decade; changes in hormone production can cause symptoms including irregular menstrual cycles, hot flashes, mood swings, and disturbed sleep.
Also known as penile curvature; a form of sexual dysfunction in which the penis is bent or curved during erection. Usually the result of fibrous scar tissue inside the penis.

The abnormal implantation of the placenta in the lower portion of the uterus, partially or completely covering the cervix. Previa means appearing before or in front of. Symptoms include painless, sudden-onset bleeding during the third trimester, and possibly also severe bleeding during delivery.

Abbreviated PCOS; a common condition characterized by an imbalance of reproductive hormones resulting in irregular menstrual cycles, hirsutism (excessive body and facial hair), and acne. High levels of insulin and the male hormone androgen are often present.
After childbirth.

Also known as pregnancy-induced hypertension; a complication of pregnancy characterized by hypertension (high blood pressure), edema, and proteinuria (an abnormally high level of protein in the urine). A common cause of preterm birth.

A painful and persistent erection lasting 4 hours or more, but is either not caused by sexual excitement or does not go away after sexual stimulation has ended. Can be caused by medications or by blood-related diseases such as sickle cell anemia or leukemia.
A woman during her first pregnancy. Compare with primipara.
A woman who has borne one viable child. Compare with primigravida.

Abbreviated SO; the surgical removal of a fallopian tube and ovary. A bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy is the removal of both of the fallopian tubes and ovaries; sometimes used to treat ovarian cancer, or to reduce the risk of ovarian cancer occurring.
breakdown_text: salping/o: fallopian tube ; oophor: ovary ; -ectomy: surgical removal

definition: A sexually transmitted disease caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum. Highly contagious and passed from person to person through direct contact with a chancre, a sore caused by syphilis. Can be detected through the VDRL blood test before the lesions appear; the RPR test is another blood test. When treated early, highly curable.

Also known as trich; an infection caused by the parasite Trichomonas vaginalis. A common symptom in infected women is a thin, foul-smelling vaginal discharge. Infected men often do not have symptoms; when present, they include painful urination or a clear discharge from the penis.

Also known as a pelvic floor hernia; a condition in which the weakening of pelvic muscles and supportive tissues allows the uterus to slide from its normal position in the pelvic cavity and sag into the vagina. Prolapse (also pronounced PROH-laps) means the falling or dropping down of an organ or internal part.
An involuntary spasm of the pelvic floor muscles, which close off the vagina. Can cause dyspareunia and difficulty tolerating the insertion of a tampon, or a speculum for a gynecological exam.
A knot of widening varicose veins in one side of the scrotum. Can lead to low sperm production and male infertility. Varicose veins are abnormally swollen veins.
breakdown_text: varic/o: varicose veins ; -cele: a hernia or swelling

definition: Also known as a vasectomy reversal; a procedure performed as an attempt to restore fertility to a vasectomized man.
breakdown_text: vas/o: blood vessel ; vas: the vas deferens ; -ostomy: surgically creating an opening

definition: A painful syndrome of unknown cause that lasts at least three months. Characterized by chronic burning, dyspareunia, itching, or stinging irritation of the vulva.

The organs of reproduction and their associated structures. External genitalia are reproductive organs located outside of the body cavity; internal genitalia are reproductive organs protected within the body.

The external surface region in both males and females between the pubic symphysis and the coccyx. In the male it extends from the scrotum to the area around the anus; in the female it extends from the pubic symphysis to the area around the anus.

The system whose primary function is to produce sperm and deliver them into the female body so that one sperm can unite with a single ovum (egg) to create a new life. Some structures also function as part of the urinary system.
The sac-like structure that surrounds, protects, and supports the testicles. Suspended from the pubic arch behind the penis and lies between the thighs.

Also known as testes; the two small, egg-shaped glands that produce the sperm (singular, testis). Develop within the abdomen of the male fetus and normally descend into the scrotum before or soon after birth.
The tubules within each testicle in which sperm are formed.

A coiled tube at the upper part of each testicle that runs down the length of the testicle, then turns upward toward the body, where it narrows to form the vas deferens. Sperm move here from the seminiferous tubules, become motile, and are temporarily stored.
Extends upward from the epididymis and is attached to each testicle. Each cord contains a vas deferens plus the arteries, veins, nerves, and lymphatic vessels required by each testicle.
Also known as sperm; the male gametes (reproductive cells).

The whitish fluid containing sperm that is ejaculated through the urethra at the peak of male sexual excitement. Formed when the seminal vesicles and the prostate gland add their secretions in the vas deferens. Ejaculate means to expel suddenly.
The process of sperm formation.
Capable of movement.

The male sex organ that transports the sperm into the female vagina. Composed of three columns of erectile tissue that fill with blood under high pressure during sexual stimulation, causing the swelling, hardness, and stiffness known as an erection.
Also known as the head of the penis; the sensitive region located at the tip of the penis.
Also known as the prepuce; a retractable double-layered fold of skin and mucous membrane that covers and protects the glans penis.
Also known as the ductus deferens; the long, narrow continuations of each epididymis that lead upward and eventually join the urethra.

Glands that secrete a thick, yellow substance to nourish the sperm cells, forming 60% of the fluid found in semen. Located at the base of the urinary bladder and open into the vas deferens as it joins the urethra.
The duct that begins at the vas deferens, passes through the prostate gland and empties into the urethra. During ejaculation, semen passes into the urethra, which exits the body via the penis.

A gland that lies under the bladder and surrounds the end of the urethra in the region where the vas deferens enters the urethra. During ejaculation it secretes a thick, alkaline fluid into the semen that aids the motility of the sperm.

Two glands located just below the prostate gland, one on either side of the urethra, that open into the urethra. During sexual arousal they secrete a fluid known as pre-ejaculate or precum that helps flush out any residual urine or foreign matter and lubricates the urethra. This fluid can contain sperm and is able to cause pregnancy even if ejaculation does not occur.
A doctor focusing on the treatment of conditions affecting male fertility and sexuality.

A physician who specializes in diagnosing and treating diseases and disorders of the genitourinary system of males and the urinary system of females. Genitourinary refers to both the genital and urinary organs.
An inflammation of the glans penis that is usually caused by poor hygiene in men who have not had the foreskin removed by circumcision.
A narrowing of the opening of the foreskin so it cannot be retracted to expose the glans penis. Can be present at birth or become apparent during childhood.
Abbreviated ED; also known as impotence; the inability of the male to achieve or maintain a penile erection. A penis that is not erect is referred to as being flaccid, or limp.
A condition in which the male reaches climax too soon, usually before or shortly after penetration.
Also known as an undescended testicle; a developmental defect seen in newborns in which one or both of the testicles have failed to descend into their normal position in the scrotum.
breakdown_text: crypt: hidden ; orchid: testicle ; -ism: abnormal condition

definition: Cancer that begins in the testicles. The most common cancer in American men between the ages of 15 and 35 years; highly treatable at all stages.
A sharp pain in the scrotum caused by twisting of the vas deferens and blood vessels leading into the testicle. Torsion means twisting.
Also known as testitis; inflammation of one or both testicles.
A sperm count of below 15 million/mL; also known as a low sperm count and a common cause of male infertility. A normal sperm count is 15 to 200 million or more sperm per milliliter of semen.
breakdown_text: olig/o: few ; sperm: sperm ; -ia: abnormal condition

definition: Also known as a sperm analysis; the testing of freshly ejaculated semen to determine the volume plus the number, shape, size, and motility of the sperm.
A self-help step in early detection of testicular cancer by detecting lumps, swelling, or changes in the skin of the scrotum.
The surgical removal of the foreskin of the penis. An optional procedure usually performed within a few days of birth, sometimes for religious reasons.
The removal of a portion of an enlarged vein to relieve a varicocele.
breakdown_text: varic/o: varicose vein ; cel: swelling ; -ectomy: surgical removal

definition: Any procedure rendering an individual (male or female) incapable of reproduction.
Also known as castration; the surgical removal or destruction of both testicles.

The male sterilization procedure in which a small portion of the vas deferens is surgically blocked or cut. Prevents sperm from entering the ejaculate but does not change the volume of semen created by the body.

Allows a man to freeze his sperm indefinitely to use later for in vitro fertilization, intrauterine insemination, or sperm donation. Sometimes done to store sperm prior to treatment for testicular cancer, which can impact fertility.
Drugs such as Viagra used to treat erectile dysfunction by causing vasodilation in the penis.

Abbreviated STDs; also known as sexually transmitted infections (STIs); infections caused by either bacteria or viruses that affect both males and females. Commonly spread through sexual intercourse or other genital contact. A common term is venereal disease, a reference to Venus, the Roman goddess of love. There are more than 20 types.
A condition caused by the bacteria responsible for chlamydia or gonorrhea. All newborns receive an antibiotic ointment in each eye within an hour after birth to prevent it.

Abbreviated BV; a condition in women in which there is an abnormal overgrowth of certain bacteria in the vagina. Not an STD, however the risk seems to increase with multiple sexual partners. Can cause complications during pregnancy and an increased risk of infection if exposed to HIV.
breakdown_text: vagin: vagina ; -osis: abnormal condition or disease

definition: Caused by the herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) or herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2). Symptoms include itching or burning before the appearance of lesions (sores) on the genitals or rectum. Highly contagious, even when visible lesions are not present. Antiviral drugs ease symptoms and can suppress future outbreaks; currently there is no cure.

Caused by human papillomaviruses (HPV), which are highly contagious. In the male, the virus infects the penis, scrotum or anus; in the female, it infects the external genitalia, cervix, and vagina. Increases the risk of cervical cancer. An HPV vaccine is available to prevent the spread of this disease.
Abbreviated HIV; transmitted through exposure to infected body fluids, particularly through sexual intercourse with an infected partner.
A sore caused by syphilis.
Venereal Disease Research Laboratory; a blood test that can detect syphilis before the lesions appear.
Rapid Plasma Reagin; a blood test for syphilis.

The system whose primary function is the creation and support of new life. The ovaries produce mature eggs to be fertilized by the sperm, the uterus provides the environment and support for the developing child, and after birth the breasts produce milk to feed the child.
A rounded, fleshy prominence located over the pubic symphysis. The external female genitalia are located posterior to it.
Also known as the pudendum; the collective term for the external female genitalia, consisting of the labia, clitoris, Bartholin's glands, and vaginal orifice.
The vaginal lips that protect the other external genitalia and the urethral meatus (singular, labium).
An organ of sensitive, erectile tissue located anterior to the urethral meatus and the vaginal orifice.
Two small, round glands located on either side of the vaginal orifice that produce a mucus secretion to lubricate the vagina.
The exterior opening of the vagina. Orifice means opening.

A thin mucous membrane that partially covers the vaginal orifice and can be torn either during the first instance of intercourse or other activity. Can be absent in a woman who has not been sexually active.

Made up of fat, connective tissue, and the mammary glands. Each breast is fixed to the overlying skin and the underlying pectoral, or chest, muscles by suspensory ligaments. The word parts mamm/o and mast/o both mean breast.
Also known as the lactiferous glands; the milk-producing glands that develop during puberty.
Also known as milk ducts; carry milk from the mammary glands to the nipple.
The dark-pigmented area that surrounds the nipple through which breast milk flows.
A pair of small, almond-shaped organs located in the lower abdomen, one on either side of the uterus. Also produce the sex hormones estrogen and progesterone.
A fluid-filled sac containing a single ovum (egg). There are thousands of these sacs on the inside surface of the ovaries.
Also known as eggs; the female gametes (singular, ovum). Immature ova are present at birth; normally, after puberty, one ovum matures and is released each month.

Also known as uterine tubes; two tubes that extend from the upper end of the uterus to a point near but not attached to an ovary. Each month, one of these tubes carries a mature ovum from the ovary to the uterus; they also carry sperm upward from the uterus toward the descending mature ovum so that fertilization can occur.
The funnel-shaped opening into the fallopian tube near the ovary.
The fringed, finger-like extensions of the opening of the fallopian tube (singular, fimbria). Their role is to catch the mature ovum when it leaves the ovary.

Also known as the womb; a pear-shaped organ with muscular walls and a mucous membrane lining filled with a rich supply of blood vessels. Located between the urinary bladder and the rectum and midway between the sacrum and the pubic bone.
The normal position of the uterus, in which the body of the uterus is bent forward.

The bulging, rounded part of the uterus above the entrance of the fallopian tubes. Because it rises during pregnancy, measuring the fundal height in relation to the pubic bone helps determine the baby's growth.
Also known as the body of the uterus; the middle portion.
Also known as the cervix uteri; the lower, narrow portion of the uterus that extends into the vagina. Within the cervix is the cervical canal, which ends at the cervical os at the vagina.
The tough, membranous outer layer of the uterus. Membranous means pertaining to a thin layer of tissue.
breakdown_text: peri-: surrounding ; metri: uterus ; -um: a singular noun ending

definition: The muscular middle layer of the uterus.
breakdown_text: my/o: muscle ; metri: uterus ; -um: a singular noun ending

definition: The inner layer of the uterus, consisting of specialized epithelial mucosa that is rich in blood vessels. Mucosa means referring to mucous membrane.
breakdown_text: endo-: within ; metri: uterus ; -um: a singular noun ending

definition: The muscular tube lined with mucosa that extends from the cervix to the outside of the body. The word parts colp/o and vagin/o both mean vagina.
Also known as menses; the normal periodic discharge of the endometrial lining and unfertilized egg from the uterus. The average menstrual cycle consists of 28 days, grouped into four phases.

The normal termination of menstruation in a woman during middle age. Confirmed when a woman has gone 1 year without having a period. The average age in the U.S. is now 51, although its onset can vary by 10 or more years.
Approximately days 1–5 of the cycle; the days when the endometrial lining of the uterus is sloughed off and discharged through the vagina as the menstrual flow.

Approximately days 6–12 of the cycle; after the menstrual period, the pituitary gland secretes follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), causing an ovum to mature. Estrogen stimulates the lining of the uterus to prepare itself to receive a zygote (fertilized egg).

Approximately days 13–14 of the cycle; ovulation occurs. The mature egg leaves the ovary and travels slowly down the fallopian tube toward the uterus. During this time, the female is fertile and can become pregnant.
Approximately days 15–28 of the cycle; if fertilization does not occur, hormone levels change to cause the breakdown of the uterine endometrium and the beginning of a new menstrual cycle.

The release of a mature egg from a follicle on the surface of one of the ovaries, which happens on approximately the 13th or 14th day of a woman's menstrual cycle. The ovum is then caught up by the fimbriae of the fallopian tube.

The ruptured follicle after the ovum has been released; it enlarges and takes on a yellow fatty substance. Secretes the hormone progesterone during the second half of the menstrual cycle, which maintains the growth of the uterine lining in preparation for the fertilized egg. If the ovum is not fertilized, it dies; if fertilized, it continues to secrete the hormones required to maintain the pregnancy.
Also known as sexual intercourse or copulation; during which the male ejaculates approximately 100 million sperm per milliliter of fluid into the female's vagina.
Occurs when one sperm penetrates and fertilizes the descending ovum. This union, the beginning of a new life, forms a single cell known as a zygote.
The single cell formed by the union of a sperm and an ovum (fertilized egg). After fertilization in the fallopian tube, it travels to the uterus where it is implanted.
The embedding of the zygote into the lining of the uterus.
The developing baby from implantation through the 8th week of pregnancy.
The baby in utero from the 9th week of pregnancy to the time of birth. In utero means within the uterus.
breakdown_text: fet: unborn child ; -us: a singular noun ending

definition: Twins that result from the fertilization of separate ova by separate sperm, developing into two separate embryos.
Twins formed by the fertilization of a single egg cell by a single sperm that divides to form two embryos. Each receives exactly the same genetic information from the parents.
The term used to describe a birth involving two or more infants.
The thin outer membrane that encloses an embryo. Contributes to the formation of the placenta.

A temporary organ that forms within the uterus to allow the exchange of nutrients, oxygen, and waste products between a mother and fetus without allowing maternal blood and fetal blood to mix. Does not keep chemicals, alcohol or drugs from reaching a fetus. Also produces hormones necessary to maintain the pregnancy.
The placenta and fetal membranes expelled after delivery of a newborn.
Also known as the amnion; the innermost membrane that surrounds an embryo in the uterus. Its common name is the bag of waters.
The fluid-filled space between the embryo and the amniotic sac that surrounds a developing embryo.
The liquid that protects a fetus and makes possible its floating movements.

The tube that carries blood, oxygen, and nutrients from the placenta to a developing baby. Also transports waste from a fetus to be disposed of through the mother's excretory system. Cut soon after the birth of the infant and before the delivery of the placenta.
Also known as the belly button; formed after birth where the umbilical cord was attached to the fetus.
The period of development of the baby in the mother's uterus, lasting approximately 280 days (40 weeks). Upon completion, the fetus is described as being at term.
The condition of having a developing baby in the uterus; often used interchangeably with gestation. Can also be divided into three trimesters of about 13 weeks each.
Also called the estimated date of delivery (EDD); calculated by taking the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP), adding one year, subtracting three months, and adding seven days.
The first movement of the fetus in the uterus that can be felt by the mother. Usually occurs during the 16th to 20th week of pregnancy.

Intermittent painless uterine contractions that occur with increasing frequency as the pregnancy progresses. Not true labor pains and usually infrequent, irregular, and essentially painless. Named after British doctor John Braxton Hicks, who first described them in 1872.
Capable of living outside the uterus. Viability depends on the developmental age, birth weight, and developmental stage of the lungs of the fetus.
Refers to the final stage of pregnancy just before the onset of labor.
Abbreviated AMA; refers to women who are 35 or older at the time of pregnancy. Can contribute to a higher risk of complications.
A woman who has given birth two or more times.
breakdown_text: multi-: many ; -parous: having borne one or more children

definition: Also known as childbirth; occurs in three stages: dilation, delivery of the baby, and expulsion of the afterbirth.

The first (and longest) stage, which begins when contractions last 30 to 70 seconds and come about 5 to 10 minutes apart. Changes include the gradual dilation and effacement of the cervix and the rupture of the amniotic sac.
The process by which the cervix prepares for delivery as it gradually softens, shortens, and becomes thinner.
The use of an electronic device to record the fetal heart rate and the maternal uterine contractions during labor.
Sometimes called active labor; begins when the cervix has dilated to 10 centimeters and is the delivery of the infant. Normally, the baby's head presents first (cephalic presentation or crowning).
The expulsion, or delivery, of the placenta as the afterbirth. Umbilical cord blood can be collected at this time so that its stem cells can be saved and used in future medical treatments.

The time from the delivery of the placenta through approximately the first 6 weeks after the delivery. By the end of this period, most of the changes in the mother's body due to pregnancy have resolved.
The postpartum vaginal discharge that typically continues for up to 4 to 6 weeks after childbirth. Consists primarily of blood and mucus.
The return of the uterus to its normal size and former condition after delivery. Involution means the return of an enlarged organ to its normal size.
A greasy substance that protects a fetus in utero and can still be present at birth. Made up of sebum and discarded epidermal cells from the skin of the fetus.

The greenish material that collects in the intestines of a fetus and forms the first feces of a newborn. Meconium aspiration syndrome is a condition causing breathing problems that can occur when a newborn passes meconium during labor or delivery and then inhales it via the amniotic fluid.
Abbreviated GYN; a physician who specializes in diagnosing and treating diseases and disorders of the female reproductive system.

Abbreviated CM; assists in labor and delivery. A certified nurse midwife (CNM) is an RN with specialized training in obstetrics and gynecology who provides primary care in normal pregnancies and deliveries.
An experienced birth coach, usually without formal obstetric training, hired to provide added support and guidance during labor, delivery, and the postpartum period.
A physician who specializes in diagnosing and treating disorders of the newborn. The neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) is a nursery offering specialized care for premature or ill infants.
Also known as a reproductive endocrinologist; helps infertile couples by diagnosing and treating problems associated with conception and maintaining pregnancy.

The absence of ovulation when it would be normally expected. Can be caused by high levels of stress, inadequate nutrition, obesity, or hormonal imbalances. Menstruation continues even if an ovum is not released.
breakdown_text: an-: without ; ovulation: the release of a mature egg

definition: Also called a teratoma; a benign tumor containing various tissues such as teeth, bone, skin glands or hair. Present at birth, and may be found on the face, inside the skull, on the lower back or on the ovaries. A large ovarian dermoid cyst may require surgical removal.

Cancer that originates within the cells of the ovaries. Cancer cells can break away and spread (metastasize) to other tissues and organs within the abdomen or travel through the bloodstream to other parts of the body. Difficult to detect in its earliest stages, when treatment is most effective.
Fluid-filled sacs in or on an ovary. Generally harmless unless they rupture.
An accumulation of pus in a fallopian tube, sometimes as a result of pelvic inflammatory disease.
An inflammation of a fallopian tube caused by a bacterial infection, usually as a result of an STD.

A cancerous growth that begins in the lining of the uterus and can spread to the ovaries and fallopian tubes. Symptoms include vaginal bleeding after menopause, bleeding between menstrual periods, and pelvic pain.
Also known as myomas; benign tumors composed of muscle and fibrous tissue that occur in the wall of the uterus. Not associated with an increased risk of uterine cancer.

A slow-growing squamous cell cancer caused by human papillomaviruses (HPV), which are spread through sexual contact. Pre-cancerous changes can be detected through routine Pap smear screening and treated to prevent the development of cervical cancer. An HPV vaccine works most effectively when administered at ages 11 or 12.
Also known as an incompetent cervix; refers to weakened tissue in the cervix. In pregnancy, may cause the cervix to open too soon, leading to late miscarriage or a premature birth.
Pain during sexual intercourse.

Also known as genitourinary syndrome of menopause; a thinning, drying, and inflammation of the vaginal walls caused by hormonal changes. Affects about half of all postmenopausal women and can be treated with vaginal moisturizers, lubricants, or estrogen therapy.
Also known as a yeast infection; a common vaginal infection caused by the yeast-like fungus Candida albicans. Symptoms include burning, itching, and a cottage cheese-like vaginal discharge.
An inflammation of the lining of the vagina. The most common causes are bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, and vaginal candidiasis.
An inflammation of the vulva. Possible causes include fungal or bacterial infections, chafing, skin conditions, or allergies to products such as soaps and bubble bath.
The presence of fibrous tissue and benign cysts. A common condition that usually occurs in premenopausal women. A cyst is a closed sac containing fluid or semisolid material.
A breast infection that is caused by bacteria that enter the mammary glands, most frequently during breastfeeding.

Also known as dysfunctional uterine bleeding; a condition characterized by abnormal bleeding during or outside of the menstrual period. Can be caused by fibroids, hormone problems or other conditions.
An excessive amount of menstrual flow, sometimes over a period of more than 7 days.
The occurrence of menstrual cycles more frequently than is normal. Polymenorrhea is the opposite of oligomenorrhea.
breakdown_text: poly-: many ; men/o: menstruation ; -rrhea: flow or discharge

definition: A condition in which the ovaries cease functioning before age 40 due to disease, a hormonal disorder, or surgical removal. Causes infertility and often brings on menopausal symptoms.
Abbreviated PMS; a group of symptoms experienced by some women within the 2-week period before menstruation. Symptoms can include bloating, swelling, headaches, mood swings, and breast discomfort.

Abbreviated PMDD; a condition associated with severe emotional and physical problems that are closely linked to the menstrual cycle. Symptoms occur regularly in the second half of the cycle and end when menstruation begins or shortly thereafter.
The interruption or termination of pregnancy before the fetus is viable.
Also known as a miscarriage; usually occurs early in the pregnancy and is due to an abnormality or genetic disorder.

An abortion caused by human intervention. When done for medical purposes, it is known as a therapeutic abortion. Achieved either through the use of an abortifacient medication within the first weeks after conception, or a surgical procedure called suction aspiration.
The inability of a couple to achieve pregnancy after 1 year of regular, unprotected intercourse, or the inability of a woman to carry a pregnancy to a live birth.

A life-threatening pregnancy complication characterized by Hemolysis (breakdown of red blood cells), Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelet count. Occurs in 10–20% of women with severe preeclampsia and can cause damage to the liver and blood cells.

Defines the presence or absence of the Rh antigen on red blood cells. Can cause difficulties when an Rh negative mother is pregnant with an Rh positive baby; antibodies that develop in the mother can cause anemia and other problems for the baby. If this potential problem exists, the mother is vaccinated with Rho(D) immune globulin. The abbreviation comes from the rhesus monkeys used in the experiments that led to its discovery in 1940.
Occurs when the buttocks or feet of the fetus are positioned to enter the birth canal first instead of the head.
Also known as a preemie; a fetus born before the 37th week of gestation. This is referred to as a preterm birth.
The birth of a fetus that died before or during delivery.

A mood disorder characterized by feelings of sadness and the loss of pleasure in normal activities that can occur shortly after giving birth. One cause is the rapid change in the hormone levels that occurs after giving birth. Treatment may be required if the depression is severe, or lasts beyond the two weeks of normal baby blues that often follows delivery.
A procedure in which a small amount of tissue from the lining of the uterus is removed for microscopic examination. Most often used to determine the cause of abnormal uterine bleeding.

Also known as an endovaginal ultrasound; performed to determine the cause of pelvic pain, infertility or abnormal vaginal bleeding by placing an ultrasound transducer in the vagina so that the sound waves can create images of the uterus and ovaries.
breakdown_text: trans-: through ; vagin: vagina ; -al: pertaining to

definition: Or Pap test; an exfoliative biopsy of the cervix developed by Dr. George Papanicolaou. Performed to detect conditions that can be early indicators of cervical cancer. Exfoliative means that cells are scraped from the tissue and examined under a microscope. A speculum is an instrument used to enlarge the opening of the vagina during the examination.

A test performed to detect an unusually high level of the human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) hormone in either a blood or urine specimen, which is normally an indication of pregnancy. A blood test at a doctor's office usually provides more reliable results than a home urine test.

Also known as combined screening; performed between 11 and 13 weeks of pregnancy and involves an ultrasound and a blood test. The combined results, plus the mother's age, detect if the fetus is at increased risk for a chromosome abnormality such as Down syndrome.
A measure taken to lessen the likelihood of pregnancy.
A form of hormones administered as an oral contraceptive. Other forms of this type of contraceptive are available as an injection, a skin patch, an arm implant, and a vaginally inserted ring.

A barrier contraceptive inserted into the vagina to cover the cervix, preventing the sperm from reaching and fertilizing the egg. A spermicide is a gel, lube, or foam that can be added to kill sperm, or stop sperm from moving.
Abbreviated IUD; a molded plastic contraceptive inserted through the cervix into the uterus to prevent pregnancy. A long-term, reversible form of contraception.
A contraceptive that will also prevent pregnancy when used correctly; the only contraceptive method mentioned here that will also prevent the transmission of sexually transmitted diseases.

Abbreviated HRT; the use of the female hormones estrogen and progesterone to replace those the body no longer produces during and after perimenopause. The goal is to relieve severe menopausal symptoms such as hot flashes and vaginal dryness. Estradiol and progestin are commonly used synthetic forms of estrogen and progesterone, respectively.
The surgical removal of one or both fallopian tubes.
A surgical sterilization procedure in which the fallopian tubes are sealed or cut to prevent sperm from reaching a mature ovum; sometimes referred to as having the tubes tied.
The surgical fixation of a prolapsed vagina to a surrounding structure such as the sacrum.
breakdown_text: sacr/o: sacrum ; colp/o: vagina ; -pexy: surgical fixation in place

definition: Also known as a cone biopsy; the surgical removal of a cone-shaped specimen of tissue from the cervix. Performed as a diagnostic procedure or to remove abnormal tissue.

Commonly known as a D & C; a surgical procedure in which the cervix is dilated and the endometrium of the uterus is scraped away. Performed as a diagnostic procedure to research the cause of abnormal uterine bleeding, or a treatment to remove tissue after a miscarriage, abortion, or childbirth. Curettage is the removal of material from the surface by scraping with an instrument known as a curette.
The surgical removal of uterine fibroids.
A hysterectomy in which the uterus is removed and the cervix is left in place.
The removal of the uterus, ligaments, cervix and a portion of the vagina. Most commonly performed to treat cervical cancer.
Also known as a complete hysterectomy; the uterus and cervix are removed. Can be performed through the vagina or laparoscopically through the abdomen.

Abbreviated BSO; the surgical removal of both of the ovaries and fallopian tubes, usually performed during a hysterectomy. If done before natural menopause, the patient will immediately experience surgical menopause.
Also spelled mammaplasty; a general term for a cosmetic operation on the breasts.
Mammoplasty performed to increase breast size, often for cosmetic reasons. Augmentation means the process of adding to make larger.
Mammoplasty performed to decrease and reshape excessively large, heavy breasts.

Also known as a C-section; the delivery of the child through an incision in the maternal abdominal and uterine walls. Usually performed when a vaginal birth would be unsafe for either the mother or baby.
The acronym for Vaginal Birth After a Cesarean. Many women whose baby was delivered via cesarean section are able to give birth vaginally in subsequent pregnancies.
An apparatus for maintaining an environment of controlled temperature, humidity, and oxygen concentration for a premature or ill newborn.
The science of aiding an infertile couple or individual achieve a viable pregnancy.
Abbreviated ART; describes techniques in which the eggs and embryos are treated outside the woman's body. Medication is often used to stimulate egg production before the retrieval process.

Most commonly intrauterine insemination (IUI); a technique in which sperm from a woman's partner or from a donor are introduced into the vagina or uterus during the ovulatory phase of her menstrual cycle.

Abbreviated IVF; a procedure in which mature ova are removed from the mother to be fertilized. The resulting healthy embryos are transferred into the uterus with the hope that they will implant and continue to develop as a normal pregnancy. In vitro means in an artificial environment such as a test tube.
Abbreviated ICSI; a form of IVF in which a single sperm is injected into a mature ovum. Sometimes used when a low sperm count is a factor in infertility.
A woman who agrees to become pregnant and give birth on behalf of a person or couple. Artificial insemination or surgical implantation of an in vitro fertilized egg may be used.
Refers to a person whose gender identity does not match their sex assigned at birth.
Refers to a person whose gender identity does match their sex assigned at birth.

Medical treatment that can change the physical characteristics of a transgender person. Gender reassignment surgery and hormone therapy can be used to alter the body to conform with the characteristics associated with the opposite sex.
